Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Minh Nguyen was 51 when he finally agreed to speak at length about the night the wildfire came through the edge of the town where he and his wife had been living for years. He had been working as a policy analyst, a job that suited his careful, methodical way of thinking, and on the evening the fire spread faster than anyone expected, he had been at home trying to finish some work while the air outside grew thick and sharp. At first he noticed only the smell, a smoky, burnt smell that seeped through closed windows and seemed to cling to the walls. Then came the uncertainty: alerts changing, roads closing, no one able to say with confidence which direction the fire would take. The unpredictability of it unsettled him immediately. He described standing in the house, checking his phone again and again, trying to decide whether to leave, and feeling as if every option might be the wrong one. When the order to evacuate finally came, he and his wife left in a rush, with little time to gather anything beyond essentials, and even then the route was uncertain because traffic had already begun to stall and reroute.

What stayed with Minh was not only the danger itself but how his body felt during those hours and in the days that followed. He became struck by a sense that he could not trust himself to make sound judgments in a crisis. He had always considered himself organized and levelheaded, yet in the face of the fire he had felt disoriented and slow to decide, and later he was certain that this meant he could not rely on himself when it mattered. In the months after the disaster, he found that anything making him feel physically unwell could bring him back to that same unsettled state. If he felt feverish, dizzy, or simply off, he would become uneasy in a way he found hard to shake, as though his body might be giving him another warning that he was missing. He also became especially unsettled by smoke or the smell of something burning. Passing a neighbor’s backyard fire pit, or catching even a faint odor of smoke on clothing, would draw his attention immediately and make him tense, scanning for signs that something was wrong. He did not describe these moments as dramatic; rather, he spoke of them as instantly pulling him out of the present and back into the night of evacuation, when the air itself seemed to announce danger.

Over time, Minh’s sense of the world changed in a quieter but persistent way. He found himself believing that he had to be especially careful because one never knew what could happen next. He began to watch for small shifts in his surroundings, paying close attention to weather alerts, unfamiliar smells, and any situation that seemed uncertain. In his work as a policy analyst, where sudden developments and ambiguous information were part of the routine, he became more strained by unpredictability than he had been before. Meetings that changed at the last minute, unclear instructions, or rapidly evolving deadlines left him on edge in a way that was hard to explain to colleagues. He could still perform his duties, but he did so with an increasingly braced, watchful stance, as if preparing for another abrupt change that might demand immediate action. At home, his wife noticed that he was quicker to check exits, quicker to ask questions, and slower to settle when plans shifted unexpectedly, even in small ways such as a delayed appointment or an altered route to the store.

As the months passed, he also struggled with the unsettling thought that his reactions after the fire meant something was seriously wrong with him. The intensity of his alarm, the way smoke could make his heart race, and the sense of unreality that came with feeling physically unwell all left him worried that he was losing his mind. He was reluctant to use those words, but he admitted that he had come to fear that his own responses were evidence that he was going crazy. This fear made him increasingly self-monitoring and self-doubting, and he often tested himself internally, wondering whether his thoughts were as controlled as they used to be. By the time he sought help, he was still functioning on the outside, but he no longer felt secure in his own judgment or ease in ordinary situations. What finally brought him to treatment was the growing strain of living in a state of constant caution, along with the distress of how quickly smoke, illness, or unpredictability could pull him into alarm. He came hoping to understand why those reminders remained so potent, and, more quietly, to find some reassurance that he had not permanently lost the ability to trust himself.
